verified.claim: Under Proposition 19 the parent-child exclusion applies only to a principal residence of the transferor that becomes the principal residence of the transferee, with a value limit of current taxable value plus $1,000,000 (adjusted every two years).
verified.quote: Principal residence of transferor and transferee - Value limit of current taxable value plus $1,000,000 (as biennially adjusted) - Family homes and farms

verified.claim: Proposition 19 removed the exclusion for other real property (rentals, second homes).
verified.quote: Eliminates exclusion for other real property other than the principal residence

verified.claim: Filing: homeowners' exemption within 1 year of transfer; exclusion claim within 3 years or before transfer to a third party.
verified.quote: File for homeowners' exemption within 1 year of transfer - File claim for exclusion within 3 years or before transfer to third party

verified.claim: The rule is implemented by Revenue and Taxation Code section 63.2 and has applied since February 16, 2021.
verified.quote: Revenue and Taxation Code section 63.2 (implements Proposition 19) ... Effective February 16, 2021

title: Letter to Assessors 2025/009 — Intergenerational Transfer Exclusion, Adjustment of the $1 Million Amount (March 7, 2025)

verified.claim: For transfers from February 16, 2025 through February 15, 2027 the value cap is the factored base year value plus $1,044,586.
verified.quote: for transfers that occur February 16, 2025 through February 15, 2027, the value cap will be the sum of the property's factored base year value plus $1,044,586.

verified.claim: The $1 million amount is adjusted every other February 16 by the prior calendar year's percentage change in the FHFA House Price Index for California.
verified.quote: Beginning on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 thereafter, the State Board of Equalization shall adjust the one million dollar ($1,000,000) amount described in paragraph (1) for inflation to reflect the percentage change in the House Price Index for California for the prior calendar year, as determined by the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

verified.claim: The 2025 adjustment used a 2.15 percent change for 2024; earlier amounts were $1,000,000 and $1,022,600.
verified.quote: the annual percentage change in the House Price Index for California for 2024 was 2.15 percent. Accordingly, the $1 million amount is adjusted to $1,044,586. ... February 16, 2021 – February 15, 2023 | $1,000,000 ... February 16, 2023 – February 15, 2025 | $1,022,600 ... February 16, 2025 – February 15, 2027 | $1,044,586

verified.claim: The next adjustment takes effect in February 2027.
verified.quote: The next adjustment of the $1 million amount will occur in February 2027.

title: Letter to Assessors 2026/026 — Proposition 19 Intergenerational Transfer Exclusion Frequently Asked Questions and Answers (August 3, 2026)

verified.claim: Transfers at death through a trust are covered by the exclusion rules.
verified.quote: Transfer — any transfer of the present beneficial ownership of a family home or family farm between a parent and a child or between a grandparent and a grandchild. This includes transfers occurring between the living and those occurring due to death, whether within or outside a trust.

verified.claim: Excluded amount (value cap) = factored base year value immediately before the transfer plus the adjusted $1 million; excess amount = full cash value at transfer minus the excluded amount.
verified.quote: Excess Amount — the full cash value of the principal residence or family farm on the date of transfer minus the "excluded amount." ... Excluded Amount — the factored base year value of the principal residence or family farm immediately prior to the date of transfer, plus $1 million. The $1 million is adjusted on February 16, 2023, and every other February 16 thereafter. Also known as the "value cap."

verified.claim: When market value exceeds the cap, the new taxable value is the factored base year value plus the excess, and it then grows by the annual inflation factor.
verified.quote: If the full cash value on the date of transfer exceeds the value cap, the amount above the value cap is added to the factored base year value, resulting in a new taxable value. A new taxable value is to be annually adjusted by an inflation factor, as provided in section 51(a).

verified.claim: The home must become the transferee's principal residence within one year, with no exceptions.
verified.quote: Yes, the transfer is required to be of a principal residence of the transferor that qualifies as the principal residence of the transferee within one year after the transfer under section 63.2(a)(1)(A). There are no exceptions to this rule.

verified.claim: A principal residence is the transferor's true, fixed and permanent home, eligible for the Homeowners' Exemption through the transferor's ownership and occupation.
verified.quote: A principal residence is defined in section 63.2(e)(5) as a dwelling that is eligible for a Homeowners' Exemption or a Disabled Veterans' Exemption as a result of the transferor's ownership and occupation of the dwelling. A principal residence is a person's true, fixed, and permanent home and principal establishment to which the owner, whenever absent, intends to return.

verified.claim: If the child later stops using the home as a principal residence, the exclusion is removed and the date-of-transfer market value (factored for inflation) is enrolled on the following lien date.
verified.quote: the exclusion will be removed as of the date the eligible transferee or subsequent eligible transferee is no longer eligible for either exemption. The value to be enrolled on the lien date following the date the exclusion no longer qualifies is the full cash value established as of the change in ownership date (new base year value), adjusted annually for inflation (factored)

verified.claim: A child who already keeps another home as a principal residence cannot qualify two homes; a home the child does not occupy is reassessed to full cash value at the transfer date.
verified.quote: only one can qualify as the child's principal residence and thus qualify for the intergenerational transfer exclusion. ... if the qualifying child does not occupy the parent's second principal residence, it will be ineligible for the intergenerational transfer exclusion and will be reassessed to its full cash value as of the date of purchase or transfer.

verified.claim: Two filings are needed: the Homeowners' Exemption within one year, and the exclusion claim within three years or before a transfer to a third party; late claims get prospective relief only.
verified.quote: the transferee must file for the Homeowners' or Disabled Veterans' Exemption within one year of the date of purchase or transfer to be considered timely. The transferee must also file for the appropriate intergenerational transfer exclusion within three years of the date of purchase or transfer, or before a transfer to a third party, whichever is earlier. ... If all deadlines have expired and the transferee still owns the property, the transferee may file a claim and receive prospective relief only.

verified.claim: For a multi-unit building, only the unit the parent occupies as a principal residence can qualify; the other units are reassessed (relevant to the next-generation transfer of the 3-unit property).
verified.quote: No, only the unit occupied as the principal residence qualifies as the principal residence of the transferor. The remainder of the apartment complex would be ineligible for the intergenerational transfer exclusion and would be reassessed at its full cash value as of the date of transfer.
